title: Your teacher
hook: the value of a living teacher

segments.voice: Yesterday, your school. Your line: know your school. Did you look up one ruling, and notice who it came from? A school is carried by people. Today, one of those people. Day one thousand four hundred three.

The companions are sitting with the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, when a stranger walks in. His clothes are bright white, his hair very black, and there's no dust of travel on him. Nobody knows him. He sits down so close that his knees touch the Prophet's knees, rests his hands on his thighs, and starts asking questions. What is Islam? What is faith? What is excellence? After he leaves, the Prophet tells them who it was: Jibril, who came to teach you your religion. That is how Sahih Muslim tells it. Notice the shape of it. Knee to knee. Today, the value of a living teacher.
screen: `A STRANGER WITH NO DUST ON HIM.` → `KNEE TO KNEE.` → `HE CAME TO TEACH YOU.`

segments.voice: First, look at how the lesson was given. Jibril could have left a scroll. Instead, the religion was taught as a conversation between two people sitting close, with questions, answers, and witnesses who carried it on. Next, the Qur'an itself travels this way. It is a recitation, heard and repeated. A student sits with a teacher who listens and corrects a vowel, a pause, a letter held too short. In Sahih al-Bukhari the Prophet says the best of you are those who learn the Qur'an and teach it. Learning and teaching sit in the same sentence. Third, even a prophet went looking for a teacher. In surah al-Kahf, Musa travels to find a servant of God who has been given knowledge, and asks to follow him so that he may be taught. The man warns him that he won't have the patience. And the story that follows is a lesson in exactly that: a student who keeps interrupting, and a teacher who bears with him twice before they part. So a teacher is not only someone who knows more. A teacher is someone who can see you, your mistakes, your rushing, your gaps, and say so kindly. Last, how people find one today. Some study with an imam at a local mosque. Some join a class for women taught by a woman scholar. Some begin online and then look for a person they can sit with. Musa's own words are a good model for the asking: may I follow you, so that you teach me? A request, not a demand.
screen: `A LESSON GIVEN KNEE TO KNEE.` · `A RECITATION, HEARD AND CORRECTED.` · `MUSA GOES LOOKING FOR A TEACHER.` · `A TEACHER CAN SEE YOU.`

segments.voice: The practice: find a class. Before searching, sit for a moment. Breathe out slowly. Think of one thing you've tried to learn on your own and stalled on: a surah you keep stumbling through, a question you keep meaning to settle, a skill half-learned from videos. Now picture asking someone for help with it, face to face, the way Musa asked. What makes the asking hard? Pride, shyness, not wanting to look slow, not knowing whom to ask. Name it, quietly, and let it sit there without obeying it. If you pray, you can ask Allah to make the asking easier. Then one plain question: who near me could teach this? After the bell, look up one class, at a mosque, a center, or online with a real person, and write its name down. The bell holds the time.
Your teacher. A living person who learned from someone, and can sit close enough to correct you. Today's word.
Your line: find a teacher. Today, ask one question of someone who knows more than you, and listen to the whole answer. Tomorrow, your mosque. Day one thousand four hundred three.

howItsDone: Muslims study with teachers in mosques, schools and homes, especially for the Qur'an, which is learned by reciting aloud to a teacher who corrects the pronunciation; some students look for a teacher whose own learning comes through a chain of teachers.

original.note: Arabic: a teacher, one who teaches.

trapdoor: what you thought: a teacher is anyone who knows more than you.
what it means: a living person, sitting close, who listens, corrects and keeps going, the way Jibril sat with the Prophet and Musa followed his teacher.
what a scholar hears: the hadith of Jibril in Sahih Muslim, recitation passed from teacher to student, and Musa asking to follow a teacher and learn.

notes: Check the paraphrase of the hadith of Jibril (Sahih Muslim 8), including the details of his appearance and his sitting knee to knee.
Confirm Sahih al-Bukhari 5027 for 'the best of you are those who learn the Qur'an and teach it'.
Musa and the servant of God (al-Kahf 18:60–82) is paraphrased; the servant is not named in the Qur'an and the script does not name him.
The practice invites asking Allah to make the asking easier; check this does not read as a new prayer.

Editor: fixed 'a teacher who keeps going anyway' (they part after the third question, 18:78) and widened the citation to 18:60–82; 'on his own thighs' changed to 'on his thighs' (the report is ambiguous); cut the chain-of-teachers line and replaced the practice (remembering a teacher), since days 1398 and 1399 used both; the practice now names what makes asking for a teacher hard.
